passages.t: Like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet
passages.happening:
“The LORD answered Moses, ‘See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet’” (verse 1). Moses is to speak all that God commands, and Aaron will tell Pharaoh to let Israel go (verse 2).

“But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (verse 3). Pharaoh will not listen. “Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD” (verses 4-5).

“So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
The long run-up of chapters 3 to 6 is over. Now the contest begins.

God answers Moses' last objection, that he cannot speak, by giving him a role. He will be ‘like God’ to Pharaoh, and Aaron will be his ‘prophet’. This tells us what a prophet is: someone who speaks another's words. As God gives a prophet his words, Moses will give Aaron his. Moses is not being made divine. He is being given God's authority before a king who thinks he himself is a god.

Pharaoh asked in 5:2, ‘Who is the LORD?’ Verse 5 gives God's answer ahead of time: ‘the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD’. That is the purpose of everything that follows. It is not only that Israel will be freed. It is that Egypt, and Israel too, will come to know who God is.

Moses is eighty, Aaron eighty-three. This fits the later picture of Moses' life in three parts of forty years: in Egypt, in Midian, and in the wilderness, ending at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7). God calls him at an age when most of his life seemed to be behind him.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart comes up again here. The chapter notes on Exodus 4 and 9 set out how Christians read it.
passages.later:
Moses was the great prophet who spoke God's words. God promised another like him, and Peter applies the promise to Jesus: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you” (Acts 3:22). Where Moses carried God's word, Christians confess that Jesus is that Word in person (John 1:14).

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you” (Romans 9:17).
passages.asks: Moses was eighty when his real work began. Ask whether you have decided that your useful years are over, or have not yet begun. And ask what it would mean to do ‘just as the LORD had commanded’, whatever your age.

passages.happening:
God tells them that when Pharaoh says, “Perform a miracle,” Aaron is to throw down his staff “and it will become a serpent” (verse 9).

They do it. Aaron throws his staff down before Pharaoh, and it becomes a serpent (verse 10). “But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts. Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs” (verses 11-12).

“Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The word for ‘serpent’ here is different from the one in 4:3. It is the word used for the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21, and for monsters of the deep. Pharaoh's crown bore a rearing cobra, and Egyptian religion was full of serpent powers. When Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, the picture is of the LORD's power swallowing the power Egypt trusted.

The ‘magicians’ were probably lector priests, learned men who read the sacred texts in Egypt's rituals and were thought to know spells. Men like these tried to read Pharaoh's dreams in Joseph's day (Genesis 41:8). Egyptian stories celebrated them. One collection of tales, in a papyrus called Westcar, tells of court magicians who brought a wax crocodile to life and folded back the water of a lake. Much later, Jewish tradition gave names to the magicians who opposed Moses, and Paul uses those names, Jannes and Jambres.

Notice the refrain at the end: Pharaoh's heart was hard, ‘just as the LORD had said’. Here the text does not say who hardened it. It simply says it was hard.
passages.later:
Paul names these magicians as a warning to the church: “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth” (2 Timothy 3:8).

Ezekiel calls Pharaoh by the same word as this serpent: “O great monster who lies among his rivers, who says, ‘The Nile is mine; I made it myself’” (Ezekiel 29:3).
passages.hard:
How could Pharaoh's magicians copy Moses' signs? Did they have real power? The text says they did the same ‘by their magic arts’, a Hebrew word that suggests secret or hidden methods, and it does not explain more.

Readers take this in two main ways. Some think of skilled illusion and the handling of snakes, arts for which Egyptian magicians were famous, and of ways to colour water that was already available. Verse 24 notes that water could still be found by digging. Others take the text to mean that the magicians drew on real spiritual power opposed to God. Scripture elsewhere warns of real signs used to lead people away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1-3), and of false wonders worked by Satan (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

On either reading the chapter's point is the same. The magicians can copy, but only in ways that make things worse. They can add blood to Egypt; they cannot turn it back into water. Their serpents are swallowed. By the third plague they fail and say, “This is the finger of God” (8:19). Whatever their power, it is limited, and in the end it is exposed. These notes take no side on what it was.
passages.asks: The magicians could copy God's signs but could not undo the harm. Ask what powers in your own world promise much but cannot heal. And ask whether you are trusting anything that, in the end, will be swallowed up.

passages.t: ‘By this you will know that I am the LORD’
passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is unyielding; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning as you see him walking out to the water. Wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him” (verses 14-15).

Moses is to say, “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness” (verse 16). “By this you will know that I am the LORD. Behold, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood. The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water” (verses 17-18).

Aaron is to stretch his hand over all the waters of Egypt, “that they may become blood” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
‘Unyielding’ is the Hebrew word ‘heavy’. The word that described Moses' ‘heavy’ mouth now describes Pharaoh's heavy heart.

The ten plagues are carefully built. The first nine fall into three groups of three. In each group, the first plague is announced to Pharaoh early in the morning, usually at the river. The second is announced after Moses goes in to him. The third comes with no warning. The tenth stands apart. Jewish readers noticed this long ago. The Passover Haggadah, the order of the Passover meal, keeps a memory aid attributed to Rabbi Judah that groups the ten as three, three and four.

Why does Pharaoh walk out to the water in the morning? Perhaps to inspect the river, perhaps for some rite; the text does not say. What is clear is that the first plague strikes the source of Egypt's life. Nearly all Egypt's people lived within a few miles of the Nile. Its yearly flood, which Egyptians honored as the god Hapi, watered and fed the fields, and fish from the river were a staple food.

And this is the river into which Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys thrown (1:22). The river of death he made is now unfit to drink.
passages.later:
Israel sang of this later: “He turned their rivers to blood, and from their streams they could not drink” (Psalm 78:44). “He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die” (Psalm 105:29).

The plagues of Egypt return in Revelation's pictures of judgment on every power that sets itself against God: the third angel poured out his bowl “into the rivers and springs of water, and they turned to blood” (Revelation 16:4).
passages.asks: God met Pharaoh at the place Egypt trusted most. Ask what you trust most for life and security, apart from God. And ask whether God may be meeting you there, to show you that he is the LORD.

passages.happening:
“Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded; in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood” (verse 20).

“The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water” (verse 21).

“But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened” (verse 22). “Instead, Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart” (verse 23).

The Egyptians dig around the Nile for water to drink. “And seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
The first plague falls in front of Pharaoh and his court. It is not hidden.

The magicians do ‘the same things’. But think about what that means. They add more blood. They do not undo any of it. Their copying only makes Egypt's suffering worse.

Then a sad, simple line: Pharaoh ‘went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart’. He walks away. Meanwhile ordinary Egyptians are digging in the mud along the river for something to drink. This pattern will come back again and again. The king is shut up in his palace, and his people pay the price.

Some readers have linked this plague to an Egyptian text called the Admonitions of Ipuwer, which laments a land in chaos and says that the river is blood. Most Egyptologists date that text centuries before any proposed date for the exodus, and read it as a poem about a time of disorder, not a record of these events.

‘Seven full days’ the river stays struck. The narrator does not hurry.
passages.later: John tells of Jesus' first sign: at a wedding in Cana he turned water into wine, and “He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him” (John 2:11). The first plague turned water into blood and brought death; Jesus' first sign turned water into wine and brought joy. John does not draw that comparison himself, so it is an echo many readers hear, not a claim.
passages.asks: Pharaoh went into his palace and did not take it to heart, while his people dug for water. Ask whether there is a warning in your life that you have walked away from. And ask who else pays the price when you will not take something to heart.
